title: Beads and silence
hookLine: Catholics pray the rosary and keep adoration before the sacrament; the Catholic path goes deeper
tomorrow: camp 3 close: a rule of life

cards: A weekday afternoon in a nearly empty Catholic church. An elderly woman sits in the back pew, her lips barely moving. In her hands, a loop of small beads slides through her fingers.
She isn't reading anything. Her fingers know the way, the way yours know a zipper or a phone code. Maybe she's praying for a grandson.
Maybe she's just resting. Many Catholics have seen a grandmother do this, or a rosary tucked into a coffin, or hanging from a rearview mirror. Today's word is that loop of beads.

teach.b: Rosary, from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers. The beads come in tens, called decades.

teach.h: DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.
teach.b: On each large bead, the Our Father; on each small bead, a Hail Mary. Then a short prayer of praise, Glory be to the Father. Five decades make a usual rosary.
The Hail Mary opens with the angel's greeting in Luke's gospel, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women."
It goes on with words from her cousin Elizabeth and a request for Mary's prayers. But the words are only half of it.

teach.h: THE LIPS REPEAT, THE HEART LOOKS.
teach.b: While the lips repeat, the mind walks through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries: the joyful, like the birth in Bethlehem; the sorrowful, like the cross; the glorious, like the resurrection.

In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. The repetition isn't meant to be boring. Like waves, the words settle the body so the heart can look.
Many Catholics keep adoration: sitting quietly in a chapel before the consecrated bread of the Eucharist, displayed on the altar, sometimes for an hour, sometimes through the night, taking turns.
No words needed. Orthodox Christians use a knotted prayer rope with the Jesus Prayer, and some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.
Most Protestants don't pray the rosary, because they don't address prayers to Mary, and many pray without beads at all. The Catholic path on Infinite Hill goes much deeper into both.

how: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, and some keep an hour of silent adoration before the Eucharist; Orthodox Christians often pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope, and some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads.

games.q: you're an Orthodox Christian with a knotted prayer rope. on each knot, what do you most likely pray?
games.why: the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. the rope, like the rosary, keeps the hands praying.

practice: Hold something small: a rosary or prayer rope if you have one, or a smooth stone, a ring, a button, even your own fingers, one at a time. Move it slowly, one breath with each small movement.
If you pray, let each breath carry a short prayer you already know, or just a name; if you don't, let the object anchor you here.

wordCard.voice: Rosary. Latin for a rose garden: a loop of beads, decades of prayer, and scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.

orig.note: Latin: a rose garden, a garland of roses. the English word rosary comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: the hands can pray too. For those who use them, beads keep the hands busy so the heart can be still. Day one hundred fifty-five, done.
